theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain how you would assess and plan the moving and installing of a 150 kg distribution panel into a first-floor plant room.
essays.modelAnswer: First I find the panel's weight, size and centre of gravity from the maker's data, and look for lifting points. I walk the route from the delivery point to the plant room, noting doors, steps, the stairs or lift, floor condition and where we can rest. Because 150 kg is too heavy to carry by hand, I plan aids: a pallet truck or dolly on the ground floor, the goods lift or a hoist to the first floor, and a trolley with straps in the plant room. I choose enough trained people and give each a role, with one leader who calls the moves and a spotter. I write a lift plan with the weight, route, aids, roles, signals and PPE, and check the aids and their ratings. At the wall, the panel is supported on a stand or lift while it is fixed.
markingPoints: Finds weight, size, centre of gravity and lifting points
Walks and checks the route
Chooses suitable handling aids, not a hand carry
Assigns people and roles, one leader, signals
Writes the lift plan, checks aids, supports the panel while fixing

essays.stem: Describe how to unload, move, set up and pay out cable from a large cable drum safely.
essays.modelAnswer: The drum is unloaded with a ramp and control ropes, a tail-lift or a crane with a spindle through the centre hole, never dropped or rolled off the tray. It is rolled only on firm, level ground in the direction of the arrow on the flange, so the cable does not work loose, and is never rolled flat. On a slope it is controlled with ropes and people stay out of its path. Where it stops it is chocked. To pay out cable, a spindle is passed through the centre hole and the drum is raised on drum jacks or a stand so it turns freely, with a brake or a person ready to slow it so cable does not over-run. The cable is pulled off the top of the drum. Gloves and safety boots are worn throughout.
markingPoints: Unloads with ramp, ropes, tail-lift or crane, never dropped
Rolls in the arrow direction on firm ground; controls on slopes
Chocks the drum when it stops
Spindle and drum jacks so it turns freely, with a brake
PPE: gloves and boots

essays.stem: Explain how you would plan and lead a team pulling a long cable into a duct or conduit by hand.
essays.modelAnswer: I check the route first, making sure the duct or conduit is clear, smooth and has a draw wire, and I work out the cable's weight and length. I set up the drum on jacks with a spindle and brake, and place a person there to feed the cable in straight and watch for damage. I place pullers at the far end and, on long runs, people at the draw-in points. I name one person to give the commands, and agree signals or use radios so anyone can call 'stop' at once. Pullers wear gloves, hold the rope in their hands and never wrap it round a hand. We pull steadily, not in jerks. If the cable sticks, we stop and find the cause instead of pulling harder. At the end I check the cable for damage before it is terminated.
markingPoints: Checks route, draw wire, cable weight and length
Drum set up with a feeder
One person gives commands; agreed signals or radios
Safe pulling: gloves, no rope round hands, steady pull
Stops if it sticks; checks cable after

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of handling lead-acid batteries for a solar or standby power system, and explain how to move and place them safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Lead-acid batteries are heavy, often more than 25 kg each, so they cause back and hand injuries and crush feet if dropped. They hold acid, which burns skin and eyes if the case leaks or cracks. Their terminals can be shorted by a tool, watch or ring, giving sparks, burns and possibly an explosion, because charging batteries can give off hydrogen. To move them I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules. I wear safety glasses, acid-resistant gloves and safety boots, and remove metal jewellery. Terminal covers are fitted. I use the carrying handles or a battery carrier, a trolley for longer moves, and two people where needed, keeping the battery upright. They are placed on a stand that can take the total weight, in a ventilated area, with a spill kit and water for washing nearby.
markingPoints: Weight and crushing hazards
Acid burns
Short circuits and hydrogen; remove jewellery, cover terminals
PPE and safe aids (carrier, trolley, two people, upright)
Rated stand, ventilation, spill kit and washing water

essays.stem: Explain how you would get materials and equipment safely up to a roof or ceiling space, such as solar panels, cable coils or light fittings.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan so that nobody carries loads up a ladder, because they need both hands to climb. Small items go up in a tool bag or bucket on a rope. Heavier items are raised with a gin wheel and rope, a hoist, or a mobile platform, with a tag line to stop them swinging. The area below is fenced off and people wear hard hats, so nobody stands under a load. On the roof, loads are put down away from the edge and tied or weighted so wind cannot move them. Solar panels are carried by two people and not moved in gusty wind. Inside ceiling spaces, loads are placed on joists or boards, not on the ceiling board. Before starting, I check for overhead power lines near any hoisting or long items.
markingPoints: No carrying loads up ladders
Uses bucket, gin wheel, hoist or platform, with tag line
Exclusion zone below and hard hats
Secures loads on roofs against wind; two people for panels
Checks overhead lines and safe placing in ceiling spaces

essays.stem: Compare carrying by hand, a sack truck, a trolley, a pallet truck and a hoist for moving electrical materials on a building site. Say when you would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Carrying by hand suits light, small items over short distances, such as a box of outlets, if the load can be held close to the body. A sack truck suits boxes, small drums and batteries over level ground, because the load is tipped back and wheeled, not lifted. A flat trolley suits several boxes, or a panel strapped upright, along corridors. A pallet truck suits a full pallet of conduit, cable or fittings on a smooth, level floor, but it is not for slopes, rough ground or stairs. A hoist, such as a chain block or gin wheel, suits lifting heavy items up, such as transformers, or materials up to a roof. For each aid I check its rated load and condition, and secure the load so it cannot slide or tip.
markingPoints: Hand carry: light, short, close to the body
Sack truck and trolley uses
Pallet truck: pallets on smooth level floors only
Hoist: lifting heavy items or up to height
Checks rated loads and secures loads

essays.stem: Explain the risks of carrying ladders, conduit lengths and other long items, both outdoors near overhead lines and inside buildings, and how to control them.
essays.modelAnswer: Outdoors, a long metal ladder or conduit held upright or raised can touch or come close to overhead power lines and kill the person holding it. So I look up before moving or raising long items, keep them low and level, and plan routes away from lines, keeping well clear of them as the power company and the Centre's rules require. Long items are hard to control in wind. Inside buildings, the ends of long items can hit people, light fittings, glass and sprinklers when the carrier turns. Long ladders and bundles are carried by two people, one at each end, with the front end held a little high and a clear view ahead. On corners, the carriers stop and look, and someone walks ahead to warn people where needed.
markingPoints: Overhead lines: look up, keep items low, keep well clear
Wind on long items outdoors
Indoor risk: ends striking people and fittings
Two-person carry for long items, front end high, clear view
Stop at corners and use a person ahead

essays.stem: Explain how a team leader can reduce the long-term risk of back, shoulder and wrist injuries in electrical installation work, such as drilling overhead, pulling cable and carrying materials.
essays.modelAnswer: These injuries build up over time from awkward postures, repeated movements and heavy loads. For overhead drilling, I would provide a platform or tower at the right height so people are not reaching above their heads, and a drill stand or extension where possible. Tasks such as pulling cable and stripping conductors are shared and rotated, with short breaks. Materials are delivered close to where they are used, in smaller packs, and moved with trolleys and hoists rather than carried. I would train the team in safe handling and make sure tools have good grips. I would ask people to report aches early and treat them seriously, and look at the job again when they do. Planning the work this way keeps the team healthy and productive.
markingPoints: Explains that these injuries build up over time
Right access height for overhead work
Rotating tasks and breaks
Aids, small loads and deliveries near the work
Training, good tools and early reporting acted on

essays.stem: Explain how to check lifting and handling aids (chain block, hoist, trolley, drum stands) before moving heavy electrical equipment, and what to do with any faulty aid.
essays.modelAnswer: Before use I check that each aid is rated for more than the load, from its marked safe working load, and that its test tag or inspection record is in date. On a chain block or hoist I look for stretched or damaged links, a working brake, a hook with a working safety catch and no cracks or opening of the hook. On a trolley or sack truck I check the wheels, tyres, frame and straps. On drum stands I check the jacks, the spindle and that the base is level and firm. I also check that the thing it hangs from, such as a beam or gantry, is rated for the load. Any aid with a fault is not used: it is tagged out of use, reported, recorded and kept apart until it is repaired or scrapped.
markingPoints: Rated load above the load; inspection tag in date
Chain block or hoist checks: chain, brake, hook and catch
Trolley and drum stand checks
Checks the support point is rated
Faulty aid tagged, reported, recorded and quarantined

essays.stem: Describe how you would lift and fix a heavy item at height, such as an outdoor air-conditioning unit or a large light fitting, using a team and lifting aids.
essays.modelAnswer: I plan the job first, finding the item's weight and fixing points from the maker's instructions, and checking that the wall or ceiling and the brackets can hold it. The circuit that will feed it stays isolated. I choose a lift aid such as a platform lift, a hoist or a material lift, so nobody holds the full weight at height, and set up a stable tower or platform for the fixers. I brief the team: one leader, who does which job, and the signals. The area below is closed off. The item is raised slowly, steadied with a hand or tag line, and placed on the brackets or temporary support. It is fixed securely before the lift aid takes its weight off. Finally I check the fixings and clear the area.
markingPoints: Checks weight, fixing points and support strength
Uses a lift aid and a stable platform
Briefs leader, roles and signals
Closes the area below; raises slowly and steadies the load
Fixes securely before releasing the aid, then checks

practical1.title: Plan and carry out a cable drum set-up and a team cable pull
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a cable drum (or a training drum) and a run of duct or conduit with draw-in points. As a group, write a short handling plan with the drum's weight, the route, the aids, each person's role and the signals. Then roll the drum the correct way to the pull position, chock it, fit the spindle and raise it on drum jacks with a brake. Pull the cable through the run as a team: one member leads and gives the commands, one feeds at the drum, and the others pull at the far end and at draw-in points. Swap roles so each member leads or feeds once. Finish by checking the cable for damage, rewinding or coiling it, and returning the drum to store. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Cable drum (or training drum) with cable
Spindle, drum jacks or stand, brake and chocks
Duct or conduit run with draw wire and draw-in points
Radios or agreed hand signals card
Gloves and safety boots for each member
photos: The completed handling plan with roles
The drum being rolled in the arrow direction
The drum chocked and raised on drum jacks with the spindle
The feeder at the drum and the leader giving commands
Cable coming out at the far end
The drum returned to store, chocked
checklist: Helped write the handling plan with weight, route, roles and signals
Rolled and chocked the drum correctly
Set up the spindle, jacks and brake safely
Led or fed the pull with clear commands or signals
Pulled steadily, never wrapping the rope round a hand
Stopped when told and helped clear a snag safely
Checked the cable and returned the equipment
safety: Gloves and safety boots for everyone handling the drum and cable
Keep clear of the drum's path when rolling; chock it whenever it stops
Never wrap a rope round a hand; anyone may call stop
No cable is pulled into any duct that holds live cables

practical2.title: Risk assess, move and wall-mount a distribution board and move a battery set
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a distribution board or panel (dummy or training unit) and a set of batteries or battery-sized dummy weights. As a group, complete a manual handling risk assessment for both loads, including weight, route, aids, people and controls. Move the batteries with a carrier or sack truck, with terminal covers fitted, and place them on a stand. Move the board with a trolley, strapped, along the planned route, then lift it onto a training wall using a temporary support or lift aid while two members fix it. Each member takes part in at least one carry and one fixing or support role, and one member acts as spotter on each move. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Distribution board or panel (dummy or training unit) with known weight
Batteries with terminal covers, or dummy weights
Trolley with straps, sack truck or battery carrier
Temporary support, stand or lift aid
Fixings, drill and level for the training wall
Gloves, safety boots and safety glasses
photos: Batteries on the carrier with terminal covers fitted
The board strapped on the trolley on its route, with a spotter
The board held on the temporary support while it is fixed
The board fixed level on the wall
checklist: Took part in the risk assessment and named sensible controls
Used safe lifting technique and kept loads close
Used the right aid for each load and secured it
Kept battery terminals covered and handled batteries upright
Took the leader or spotter role clearly when asked
Fixed the board level and secure before the support was removed
Left the route and work area clear
safety: No one carries a load that the risk assessment says needs an aid
Remove metal jewellery and wear safety glasses near batteries
Keep the area below and around the board clear while it is lifted
Stop at once if anyone feels pain, and report it
